10.5281/zenodo.23930484.j: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
10.5281/zenodo.23930484.a: This Project Handbook (D1.1) sets out the management, quality and governance procedures that all EOSC-Marine partners follow to implement the project. It describes the governance bodies established under the Consortium Agreement, namely the General Assembly, the Steering Board, the Technical Board and the Stakeholder Advisory Board, together with their roles, composition and meeting schedule. It presents the project's collaboration tools, including the Document Management System hosted on the EOSC Node | European Digital Twin Ocean on D4Science, the mailing lists, and the project meetings. It defines the quality assurance framework for deliverables, from production and internal peer review to submission, and the procedure for publishing all project results in the EOSC-Marine Catalogue and on Zenodo, so that they are findable, citable, and onboarded into the EOSC Federation. The Handbook also sets out the risk management and contingency plan, the procedures for conflict resolution, the rules on intellectual property and confidentiality, and the principles for data management, open access and ethics. It is a living document and will be updated whenever procedures change during the project.

10.5281/zenodo.23777351.t: EOSC Node European Digital Twin Ocean: Lessons learnt and next steps
10.5281/zenodo.23777351.j: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
10.5281/zenodo.23777351.a: This presentation shares lessons learnt from bringing the EOSC Node European Digital Twin Ocean into production, providing a single entry point to federated marine data, research environments and analytical services. Building on D4Science and EDITO, and supported by EOSC-Marine, the Node demonstrates how existing infrastructures can be connected through shared authentication, interoperable catalogues and open standards. It examines practical challenges in reconciling accounting and resource-allocation models, alongside governance approaches that combine long-term infrastructure support with project-driven innovation. Operational marine services and a prospective cross-node use case on biological carbon sequestration illustrate the scientific opportunities enabled by the EOSC Federation. The presentation concludes with priorities for integration into EDITO, wider cross-node collaboration and sustainable operation, emphasising a central principle: federation should simplify researchers' work while preserving existing providers' services and processes.

10.6075/j0cchds1.t: CCHDO Hydrographic Data Archive, Version 2026-11-01. In CCHDO Hydrographic Data Archive
10.6075/j0cchds1.a: CCHDO contains hydrographic data collected from research vessels globally. Data are aggregated from science party submissions from programs such as GO-SHIP, WOCE, and CLIVAR aimed at reference-quality data. The data are assembled by cruise into several standard formats (e.g. WHP-Exchange, WOCE, and netCDF), as well as assessed for consistent parameter naming and flags, and known units of measurement. Data are not further quality controlled by CCHDO. The primary location of the CCHDO dataset is https://cchdo.ucsd.edu/. Snapshots of the CCHDO data and metadata are being deposited periodically for long-term preservation and access at the UC San Diego Library and are therefore also available through this collection. The most recent snapshot can be accessed at the top of the list of collection items. Data Formats: Data are available in CF/netCDF, WHP Exchange, COARDS netCDF, and WOCE text formats. CF/netCDF is a netCDF file following the Climate and Forecast metadata conventions available at https://cfconventions.org/, it is specifically using the incomplete multidimensional array representation of profiles defined in section 9.3.2. The WHP Exchange format is a CSV-like format described at https://exchange-format.readthedocs.io/. COARDS netCDF is an older netCDF metadata convention and uses one file per profile. The WOCE text formats, which are defined in Chapter 4 of WOCE Publication 90-1 uses separate formats for discrete and continuous data. Users of WOCE data must also download the Station Summaries, defined in Chapter 3 of WOCE Publication 90-1, for profile time and space information. File Names: All the file names in this snapshot have been regularized from what may be available on https://cchdo.ucsd.edu. All file names will start with the expedition identifier called an Expocode followed by an extension that identifies the type of data. Files and data from the same expedition will have the same Expocode. The following is a list of the extensions: * Bottle - CF/netCDF: _bottle.nc - WHP Exchange: _hy1.csv - COARDS netCDF _nc_hyd_.zip - WOCE Text: hy.txt * CTD - CF/netCDF: _ctd.nc - WHP Exchange: _ct1.zip - COARDS netCDF _nc_ctd.zip - WOCE Text: ct.zip * Large Volume - WOCE Text: lv.txt * Cruise Reports: - PDF: do.pdf - text: do.txt * Station Summaries - WOCE Text: su.txt Bottle Data: The bottle data contains data from the analysis of water samples. While most of these data are from samples collected from Niskin bottle closures, it can also include any other discrete sample that was collected on an expedition. These data also typically include the readings from CTD sensors at the time of the bottle closure. For older data, it may also include readings from reversing thermometers. These data are available in all 4 formats. CTD Data: The CTD data contain in situ readings from instruments that were lowered into the ocean. Typically only the data read while the instrument package was being lowered is included. These data are usually grouped into 1 to 2 decibar pressure bins. Data from the major programs (WOCE, CLIVAR, GO-SHIP, GEOTRACES) will have had the sensors calibrated using data from the bottle samples. These data are available in all 4 formats. Large Volume Sample Data: Eleven expeditions from WOCE reported separate large volume samples. The large volume samples were done almost exclusively for radiocarbon measurements using a device called a Gerard Barrel. Improved analysis techniques eliminated the need for separate large volume sampling so radiocarbon measurements are integrated with the rest of the bottle data. These data are only available in the WOCE text format. Cruise Reports: The cruise reports are narratives of what happened on each expedition. These will include expedition goals, techniques utilized, preliminary data reports, and reports of issues. These reports are often very useful when investigating why some data may look unusual. These reports are available in PDF and text formats. The PDF formats will include figures and images not able to be included with the text versions. Station Summaries: Station summaries contain profile information including longitude, latitude, and times. It will contain one row per event and a single profile may have multiple events. The format is defined by chapter 3 of WOCE Publication 90-1. When using WOCE text formatted CTD, Bottle, or Large Volume sample data, these station summaries must also be downloaded.

10.5194/essd-2026-860.t: SDUST2026SM: a global seamount catalog based on vertical gradient of gravity anomaly and bathymetric data
10.5194/essd-2026-860.a: Abstract. This study applies the integrated seamount detection and height estimation method based on vertical gradient of gravity anomaly (VGGA) and bathymetry (ISDHEB) to detect and catalog seamounts across the global ocean between 80° N and 80° S. This analysis uses the SWOT_04 VGGA field released by the Scripps Institution of Oceanography (SIO) and the GEBCO_2025 bathymetry grid. The global ocean was divided into 10° × 10° processing tiles, each surrounded by a 1° overlapping buffer. Candidate features were screened using multiple constraints, including local maxima, closed contours, area and amplitude, circular or elliptical fitting, Jaccard similarity, and seamount exclusion zones. Marker-controlled watershed segmentation was used to separate multi-peak anomalies. Foot-of-slope points were then identified from the slope and second derivative of bathymetric profiles to estimate base depth and seamount height, followed by visual quality control. A total of 68,934 candidate seamounts at least 100 m high were identified. Small, medium, and large seamounts accounted for 67.6 %, 30.9 %, and 1.5 % of the candidates, respectively. After visual inspection, 67,374 targets were retained in the high-confidence seamount set, corresponding to an overall candidate acceptance rate of 97.74 %. The high-confidence catalog contains 55.0 % more seamounts than the SIO 2023 catalog, with most additional targets having heights below 1 km. The cumulative height-frequency relationship follows a clear power law above 0.8 km but progressively deviates at lower heights. The expanded catalog reflects the combined benefits of SWOT-enhanced gravity information, updated bathymetry, and the integrated detection and height-estimation procedure. The resulting catalog provides a basis for studies of seafloor tectonics, shipborne bathymetric survey planning, and marine ecological and resource investigations. The SDUST2026SM dataset is publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23277209 (Gao et al., 2026).

10.71245/yfva2935.t: Global Ocean Observing System status Report 2026
10.71245/yfva2935.a: The ocean underpins the safety, wellbeing and livelihoods of communities worldwide. Understanding how it is changing depends on sustained ocean observations: the measurements collected by dedicated people, instruments and platforms, from the seafloor to the atmosphere. The Global Ocean Observing System (GOOS) Status Report 2026 provides an interactive overview of the status of the global ocean observing system, presents new statistics on national contributions, and showcases the societal value of ocean observations through impact stories from around the globe. Today, 67 countries contribute to physical and biogeochemical ocean observations at sea through 17 GOOS observing networks monitored by OceanOPS. Satellites complement these measurements with observations from space, while a diverse community of initiatives collects vital data on marine life and ecosystems. Together, these observations underpin weather forecasting, climate monitoring, maritime and coastal risk management, biodiversity conservation and sustainable ocean economies. The global ocean observing system continues to make progress, supported by established observing networks, long-term reference observatories, regional systems and emerging technologies. Yet, important gaps and risks remain. Observing capacity is unevenly distributed around the world, and many networks face challenges in securing the sustained funding needed to maintain and expand their observations. Strengthening coordination, improving data sharing and broadening international participation will be essential to build a more comprehensive, resilient and sustainable system. Continued investment and stronger collaboration across countries and observing communities are crucial to ensure that ocean observations can meet growing scientific, operational and societal needs. Explore the interactive GOOS Status Report to find out more.

10.2118/235285-ms.t: A Physics-Based Digital Twin for Real-Time Steel Catenary Riser Fatigue from Existing FPSO Motion-Reference-Unit Data, with Generalization to Fixed Jacket Structures
10.2118/235285-ms.j: Abu Dhabi International Petroleum Exhibition & Conference (ADIPEC)
10.2118/235285-ms.a: Abstract This paper establishes a physics-based digital twin that converts existing FPSO motion reference unit (MRU) data that is continuously recorded but never applied to structural integrity into real-time steel catenary riser (SCR) fatigue records. The core objectives are to derive and validate the MRU-to-touchdown-point transfer function, develop an Arabian Gulf corrected fatigue accumulation model, and to demonstrate condition-based optimized inspection for probabilistic remaining life estimation. The digital twin operates through two layers. Layer 1 uses the MRU-to-touchdown-point bending moment transfer function using lazy-wave catenary mechanics and linearized Morison loading, validated against Quéau et al. (2015, Ocean Engineering) across the frequency range 0.05 to 0.30 Hz. In Layer 2, rainflow cycles are computed and accumulated using Miner's rule on Arabian Gulf-corrected DNV S-N curves, taking a temperature factor of 0.72–0.78 (Vosikovsky 1975) and a salinity factor of 0.85–0.90 (combined factor 0.61–0.70). 10,000-member Monte Carlo ensemble maps uncertainties into a continuous remaining fatigue life probability distribution. Applied to typical SCR configurations subject to Arabian Gulf wave climate conditions, with North Sea reanalysis incorporated as a reference operating environment, the digital twin generates three findings. Firstly, realistic interannual wave climate variability leads to an observed discrepancy in accumulated fatigue damage fraction prediction between design and simulation of 5% at the 10th ensemble percentile and 28% at the 90th percentile by year 15, indicating that static design calculations are inherently unreliable for each asset individually. Secondly, the 90% credible interval for remaining fatigue life narrows proportionately to 1/√T, where T is the monitoring period, consistent with Bayesian posterior contraction, and is halved after four years of continuous MRU monitoring. Thirdly, the Arabian Gulf environmental correction reduces effective SCR fatigue life by 30–39% compared to standard DNV seawater curves, indicating a non-conservative allowance that will be systematically underestimated using North Atlantic calibrated design calculations for Arabian Gulf assets. Condition-based inspection scheduling guided by digital twin output projects a 20-year net inspection cost reduction of $6.6M to $36.5M for a 20-unit floating production fleet, with sensor network investment recovered within one to six years

10.1186/s40623-026-02566-w.t: A shallow prominent reflector in seawater identified using the seismic oceanographic method off the east coast of the Noto Peninsula, Japan Sea
10.1186/s40623-026-02566-w.a: We conducted a seawater imaging study using multichannel seismic reflection (MCS) data acquired off the eastern coast of the Noto Peninsula in the Japan Sea following the 2024 Noto Peninsula earthquake ( M J 7.6). A shallow prominent reflector (SPR) was identified within the water column of the Toyama Trough. The SPR exhibited significant spatial variations, appearing as a continuous, high-amplitude reflection in select areas while appearing weak and discontinuous in others. To investigate the mechanisms underlying the formation of this reflector, we compared MCS images with concurrently collected conductivity, temperature, and depth (CTD) data. The results suggest that the SPR was generated by a notable change in the acoustic impedance associated with a high vertical density gradient within the pycnocline, which functions as a transition layer between the surface mixed layer and the underlying Japan Sea Proper Water. We conclude that the spatial variations in the characteristics of the SPR could be controlled primarily by changes in the thickness of the surface mixed layer driven by wind-induced mixing, eventually affecting the magnitude of the vertical density gradient. These findings demonstrate the potential of MCS data for visualizing upper-ocean stratification and mixed-layer variability in the Japan Sea.

10.3389/fmars.2026.1941879.t: Toward ocean practices sustainability - an evolution of the Ocean Practices Maturity Model
10.3389/fmars.2026.1941879.a: Global challenges such as climate change, ecosystem sustainability, and marine food resources require widely adopted practices for observation, data management, and application that produce the consistent, interoperable information needed for informed decision-making. Identifying mature, sustained practices helps build the broad acceptance needed for widespread adoption. This paper reviews the original Ocean Practices Maturity Model (OPMM) and presents an updated version, OPMM2, developed through co-design with the ocean research and applications community. OPMM2 offers clearer metrics for maturity levels across a wide range of ocean activities, along with a standardized set of definitions for both Level Attributes and the associated vocabulary. The result is clear guidance for advancing a practice from Documented to Adopted to Sustained. OPMM2 was co-designed and evaluated through personal interviews with authors representing a wide range of ocean practices. These practices spanned physical oceanography, biogeochemistry, and biology/ecosystem disciplines, as well as platforms, sensors, data management, and fisheries. As a result, OPMM2 is being adopted as the maturity framework for inclusion and discovery by methodology repositories. Additional impact is emerging as authors revise their practice documents to include opportunities for further maturity advancement in areas such as user feedback and training.

10.5281/zenodo.23761302.j: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
10.5281/zenodo.23761302.a: MPA Solutions Hub: Frontend (SPA) This repository contains the frontend component of the MPA Solutions Hub, a core result of the BLUE4ALL Horizon Europe project. The platform is a practical, co-created tool for effective management of Marine Protected Areas (MPAs), aligning top-down policy objectives with bottom-up stakeholder perspectives. Development was driven by extensive engagement through 12 Information Sites and 13 Living Labs across European sea basins, ensuring that the tools and guidance are tested against real management needs. ArchitectureThe platform follows an open and adaptive architecture, combining a single-page web application (SPA) with a RESTful backend and a flexible database structure. This design supports advanced search, filtering and tool interoperability. This deposit covers the SPA only; the backend and database layers are not included. Contents Source code of the SPA (user interface, search and filtering views, integration with the RESTful API) Build and configuration instructions (see README) Third-party license notices RequirementsA running instance of the MPA Solutions Hub RESTful API is needed for full functionality. Environment variables are provided as placeholders; no credentials or production endpoints are included. FAIR and open accessAll resources are developed in line with FAIR data principles and open-access standards. LicenseGNU General Public License v3.0 or later. Logos and branding assets of BLUE4ALL, the European Union and partner organisations are excluded from this license and remain the property of their respective owners. 10.36038/0131-6184-2026-5-60-69.t: Cognitive Digital Ocean: integration of quantum hybrid computing, digital twins and graph neural networks for bioresource and fleet management. Part 2
10.36038/0131-6184-2026-5-60-69.a: The paper presents the concept of the Cognitive Digital Ocean (CDO) – a multi level cyber physical system for managing the fishery complex, integrating quantum hybrid computing, physics informed neural networks (PINN), graph neural networks (GNN), a hierarchy of digital twins (from genome to global ocean), and fractal analysis of the spatial distribution of bioresources. Special attention is paid to the shipbuilding aspect: mathematical models of the ship power plant (SPP), controllable pitch propeller (CPP), propulsion complex, and hull hydrodynamics are presented. It is shown that solving the fundamental Millennium Problem – the Navier Stokes equations – on quantum computers opens up fundamental possibilities for hydrodynamic forecasting with a horizon of up to 30 days. The system is aimed at solving the strategic tasks of the Russian Federal Agency for Fisheries (Rosrybolovstvo) until 2030: increasing production by 25%, digital transformation, and technological sovereignty. The limitations of the applicability of quantum methods are considered and engineering workarounds are proposed.
